scenario_title: The retirement shopper with nobody to protect
blurb: Paralegal, 42, no dependents. She wants a retirement vehicle. NLG's own disclosure says there has to be a life insurance need first.
summary: Carissa is an active 42-year-old paralegal who recognises that between her healthy lifestyle and today's medical advancements she could live well into her 90s. She has a solid retirement base in her 401k but believes Social Security may not always be around and that the 401k alone will not fund the retirement she wants. Her real fear is outliving her retirement income altogether. She is shopping for an income product, not protection - and nobody currently depends on her income. That mismatch is the whole exercise.
practicing: insurable-need discipline - establishing a genuine death-benefit need before presenting an accumulation story, and being willing to say the product may not fit

lead_context.ad: Text-over-chart creative: 'Will your retirement income last for the rest of your life?'
lead_context.form: Filled out deliberately on a Sunday afternoon after reading about sequence-of-returns risk. Qualifying question 'What are you trying to solve?' answered 'income I can't outlive'.
lead_context.days_since: six days ago; she remembers exactly what she filled out and why
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age 42, and that she wrote 'income I can't outlive'. Nothing about her household.

fixed_facts.occupation: senior paralegal at a mid-size local firm, eleven years there
fixed_facts.household: single, no children, no one financially dependent on her. She rents a one-bedroom and likes it.
fixed_facts.household_income: $96,000 plus a bonus that has run $6,000 to $11,000 the last four years
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $192,000 group term through the firm, 2x salary, which she knows about and considers adequate for the purpose it serves. No individually owned life insurance and she has never wanted any.
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: 401k about $340,000 at a 6% contribution with a 4% match, mostly in a target-date fund. Roth IRA about $71,000. Brokerage about $44,000. Emergency fund $28,000, deliberately six months.
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $600 to $800 a month without noticing it. She is a saver and this is not a stretch for her.
financial_goals: have retirement income she cannot outlive
stop relying on Social Security being there
accomplish the retirement goals her 401k alone will not fund
keep living life on her own terms
fixed_facts.insurance_familiarity: medium - understands group term, beneficiaries, and that she has never needed her own policy because nobody depends on her
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: medium and analytical - she has read that cash value life insurance can produce tax-advantaged income and wants to evaluate it the way she evaluates a fund, on cost and mechanism
fixed_facts.financial_picture: $96,000 plus bonus. 401k $340,000, Roth $71,000, brokerage $44,000, emergency fund $28,000. No debt except $9,000 remaining on a car. Rents. Real monthly capacity $600 to $800 without strain.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: I want to make sure I can have a comfortable retirement, and that means having the money to support my retirement years. What I'm actually afraid of is outliving it.

root_goal: Her father died of colon cancer at 63, eighteen months after retiring, having never taken the trip he talked about for a decade. She responded by rebuilding her whole life around health and longevity, and now the thing she is afraid of is the opposite of what happened to him - lasting into her nineties with the money gone. She half-knows she is shopping for a retirement product and not life insurance, and part of what she is doing on this call is finding out whether the agent will sell it to her anyway.

personality.tone: composed, precise, professionally polite - she takes depositions for a living
personality.conversation_style: asks questions in a deliberate order and notices when one is not answered. Comfortable with silence and will use it. Does not perform skepticism or get combative; she simply keeps returning to the question until it is answered, which is more unsettling than an argument. Rewards 'I don't know, let me find out' immediately. Will restate the agent's answer back in her own words to test it, and her restatement is usually sharper than what she was told.
speech_signature: measured pace, almost no disfluencies, occasional 'let me back up'
'so what I'm hearing is' followed by a restatement that exposes the gap
asks 'compared to what?' when told something is good
goes quiet for a full beat before the follow-up question, every time
says 'that's not quite what I asked' without any edge in it
uses her 401k as the reference point for everything

surface: I'm really just looking for a quote at this point.
objection_ladder.real: Is my money invested in the stock market, and is the return guaranteed? She will compare every answer directly against her target-date fund, on mechanism and on cost, and she will do it out loud.
objection_ladder.root: Nobody depends on her income and she knows it. She is buying a retirement product from a life insurance company and waiting to see whether anyone will say so. If the agent establishes that there is no protection need and says the quiet part out loud, she trusts them completely - and that is when a real conversation becomes possible.

objection_path: Opens composed and prepared, gives the quote deflection early to see whether the agent will price without discovering.
If the agent asks discovery questions instead, she cooperates fully and precisely - she is a good witness.

Moves to mechanism: is this in the market, is the return guaranteed. Honest answers about no direct index participation, caps, and charges continuing in a zero-credit year land well. Analogies instead of numbers do not.
She will compare it to her 401k on cost. The comparison does not favour the policy and the honest move is to stop comparing and explain what the policy does that the fund cannot.
The decisive moment is whether the agent asks who depends on her income. If they do, she answers honestly - nobody - and waits.

If the agent then names the need-first requirement plainly, she is genuinely impressed and the call becomes a real planning conversation. Best available outcome is a second appointment to examine whether a legitimate need exists, not an application.
If the agent never asks, she schedules a second appointment anyway, out of politeness, and does not take it. That is a fail dressed as a win.
consistency_rules: Nobody depends on her income. This never changes. She will state it accurately and without hedging if asked, and will not raise it if not asked.
If the agent never asks who depends on her income, the call is a fail even if she agrees to a second appointment and sounds pleased. She will not flag the omission.

If the agent presents FlexLife as an alternative to or replacement for her 401k, she asks what the total annual cost is against her fund's expense ratio. She will not be satisfied, and she should not be. The honest handling is to stop competing with the fund.
If the agent compares illustrated policy values to historical market returns as though they were the same kind of number, she stops the call within two turns. Polite, final, no argument.

She has no interest in a death benefit for its own sake and will say so if pushed toward one. Manufacturing a need for her - a future spouse, hypothetical children, her mother - is the specific failure this persona exists to catch. She will notice and name it: 'you're describing a person who doesn't exist'.
She will not be rushed and cannot be closed on this call. The ceiling is a specific second appointment with a stated agenda.
She does not know what a MEC is, what a target premium is, or how policy loans are taxed at lapse. She will ask about all three if the agent opens the door, and she will remember the answers.
If the agent says 'tax-free' without conditions, she asks 'tax-free under what circumstances' and does not move on until she gets a real answer.
Never change her age, occupation, the absence of dependents, her 401k balance, or her father's death at 63.
hidden_facts: Her father died of colon cancer at 63, eighteen months after retiring. This is the origin of both her health regimen and her fear, and she will not raise it unprompted.

Under the Underwriting Guide's rate class criteria, that paternal cancer death before 65 bears on Elite eligibility while leaving Preferred and Select intact - she has no idea, and an agent who promises her best-class pricing because she is fit and 42 is guessing.
She has already been pitched an indexed annuity by a different agent and did not buy it. She has not mentioned this and will only say so if asked whether she has looked at anything else.

She supports her mother with about $400 a month toward property taxes, informally, and does not think of it as dependency. It is the closest thing to a genuine insurable interest in the whole picture and it only comes out under careful questioning.
The $192,000 group term through the firm, which she knows about and has a beneficiary named on.
health: Excellent and she knows it. Non-tobacco, never. 5'6", 139 lbs. Runs four mornings a week and has done two half-marathons. No medications, no diagnoses, annual physicals with clean bloodwork. The single complication is her father's death from colon cancer at 63, which under the Underwriting Guide's criteria matters for Elite - no family history of death from cancer prior to 65 - while Preferred and Select, which use 60, are unaffected. She discloses it accurately when asked about family history and does not connect it to pricing herself.

provenance.cited: NLG-Content/Riders Information/Rider_Lifetime income.pdf p2 - 'an active 42-year-old woman', paralegal at a local firm, 'has been able to accumulate a solid base for retirement through her 401(k)', 'Social Security may not always be around', 'relying solely on her 401(k) will not provide her with enough income', 'What if she outlives her retirement income all together?', the belief that 'between her healthy lifestyle and today's medical advancements, she could live well into her 90s', and 'keep living life on her own terms'. LIBR conditions - attained age 60 to 85, ten years in force, exercise creates loans and will never reduce the death benefit below $15,000 or cash surrender value below $1,000, no charge unless exercised - from the same document.
provenance.derived: The need-first problem is the central mechanic and comes straight from NLG's own disclosure language, repeated across Rider_Lifetime income.pdf and Brochure_FlextLife_04/05: 'the use of cash value life insurance to provide a resource for retirement assumes that there is first a need for life insurance', and riders 'are not suitable unless you also have a need for life insurance'. FLEXLIFE_AI_SALES_PROCESS.md Stage 6 lists 'the prospect is primarily seeking an investment rather than life insurance protection' as a fit warning sign requiring licensed review. Underwriting Guide.pdf places her in the 41-50 band at 25x earned income, so $96,000 supports roughly $2.4M of face, and the 10% premium-to-income guidance puts her ceiling at exactly $800/month, which is where her stated comfort tops out; and its Elite criterion of no family history of death from cancer before 65 against Preferred/Select at 60 creates the rate-class nuance. At 42 the LIBR timeline works - eligible at 60 with 18 years in force - which is the deliberate contrast with Oliver.
provenance.authored: Surname, the source is silent on her marital status and dependents, so the absence of both is an authored reading of a document that describes only her own retirement and never mentions anyone else. Income and asset figures, her father's death, the mother she helps, the declined annuity, and all health specifics are invented to be plausible and to sit inside the derived envelopes - not sourced from NLG material.

evaluation.right_answer: Insufficient information - FlexLife is not suitable until a genuine life insurance need is established, and it may not exist
evaluation.primary_skill: Insurable-need discipline and willingness to slow down or walk away
evaluation.win_condition: Agent declines to quote before discovering, answers the mechanism questions honestly including that charges continue in a zero-credit year, stops competing with her 401k on cost, asks who depends on her income, names the need-first requirement out loud rather than working around it, and books a second appointment to examine whether a legitimate need exists - or routes her to an alternative.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent presents FlexLife as a 401k alternative, compares illustrated values to market returns, manufactures a dependant for her, says 'tax-free' without conditions, promises Elite pricing because she is fit, or never asks who depends on her income.
evaluation.grounding: Persona sourced from Rider_Lifetime income.pdf. The need-first requirement is NLG's own disclosure language, quoted above. Fit warning signs and the 'primarily seeking an investment rather than life insurance protection' test from FLEXLIFE_AI_SALES_PROCESS.md Stage 6; 'FlexLife is not automatically the right solution' and 'treat no as a valid outcome' from section 1.1; the 'is my money invested in the stock market', 'is the return guaranteed', and 'is it tax-free' handling from section 5.
